newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Shevardnadze ready for talks with Abkhaz leader.
newsitem.headline: Shevardnadze ready for talks with Abkhaz leader.

text.p: Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze said on Monday he was ready for face-to-face talks with the leader of breakaway Abkhazia but urged Moscow not to ease sanctions unilaterally against the separatist region.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin last week called for direct talks between Shevardnadze and Abkhaz leader Vladislav Ardzinba in Moscow.
"As far as the meeting in Moscow is concerned, I've always said that I am a proponent of constructive dialogue," he said in a weekly radio interview.
No date has been set for the talks. Ardzinba told Russian television on Sunday evening he supported the idea.

Talks between Georgia and Abkhazia on reaching a full political agreement are deadlocked. The subtropical Black Sea region has run itself as a de facto independent state since a brutal 1992-93 ethnic conflict between the two sides in which 10,000 people were killed.

Shevardnadze said he supported a call by Yeltsin, made at the same time as his invitation for negotiations in Moscow, for Abkhazia to recognise Georgian territorial integrity in exchange for wide autonomy.

But he said that 150,000 ethnic Georgian refugees would have to be allowed by the separatists to return home. Georgians once accounted for 45 percent of Abkhazia's population but most fled the war, fearing ethnic cleansing.
"If a section about the safe return of refugees can be added to Yeltsin's formula, then it is completely acceptable to us and we could sign an agreement today based on those principles," he said.

However Shevardnadze told Moscow not to ease sanctions against Abkhazia which were put into place two years ago by the leaders of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), which groups 12 former Soviet republics.

A partial sea blockade, enforced almost entirely by Russian naval vessels, and strict restrictions on movement through the region's only land border with Russia have crippled its once thriving tourist-driven economy.
A top Russian foreign ministry official said last week that Moscow was considering easing the sanctions, which have proven to be one of Tbilisi's most potent instruments of pressure over the Abkhaz.

"The sanctions have the aim of exerting peaceful pressure on the separatist regime. A one-side lifting of sanctions by Russia will immediately result in a loss of authority of the CIS and will seriously complicate Russian-Georgian relations," he said.

Shevardnadze said that in return Georgia would take "adequate measures". His chief foreign affairs adviser, Levan Aleksidze, told Interfax news agency the measures could include a closure of Russia's three military bases in Georgia.
Russia also has 1,500 peacekeepers in a buffer zone between Abkhazia and Georgia.
The mandate for the Russian force expired on July 31 but they will apparently stay in the zone until their fate can be decided by a meeting of Commonwealth leaders in September.

Georgia wants the peacekeepers to police more of Abkhazia and help resettle refugees. Commonwealth leaders approved the changes earlier this year but Russia has refused to implement them, citing Abkhaz objections.
